newsitem.title: ITALY: Candidates square up in election for Milan mayor.
newsitem.headline: Candidates square up in election for Milan mayor.

text.p: A mayoral election this Sunday in Milan may deliver a shot in the arm -- or a slap in the face -- for Prime Minister Romano Prodi's struggling centre-left Olive Tree coalition in Rome.

The Milan vote is the most important test in elections for mayors and councillors in more than 1,100 cities and towns and a barometer of the national mood. Like many of the other contests, it is expected to go to a second round run-off on May 11.
"It is hard to say whether national or local issues will prevail but my feeling is that in Milan local problems may have the upper hand," said Renato Mannheimer, a leading Italian opinion pollster.

The Olive Tree coalition and the centre-right Freedom Alliance, led by Milanese media magnate Silvio Berlusconi, are both fielding candidates in a bid to oust the current mayor, Marco Formentini, who is running for a second term.
Formentini rode to victory four years ago at the head of the separatist Northern League party on a wave of popular disgust with the old political order.

He is now thought by many Milanese to have failed to deliver on a promise to revive the city's fortunes but political analysts say he cannot be counted out because of widespread public disenchantment with the main national political parties.

A huge web of corruption linking top politicians to big business was uncovered by magistrates in Milan in 1992, sending shockwaves throughout the country and triggering the collapse of the old party system.
The Tangentopoli (Bribesville) investigation left deep scars in Milan, just as the economy was losing its fizz in the early 1990s, helping to undermine a once indomitable self-confidence.
A poll carried out in January showed more than three quarters of the city's 1.3 million inhabitants believed quality of life in the city had deteriorated over the past 10 years.
In another recent survey, more than half of those polled said they would move out of the city if given the opportunity.
Critics of Formentini's administration accuse him of lacking vision and of a failure to tackle chronic traffic congestion which has led to steadily worsening atmospheric pollution.
Plans have also stalled to find a temporary home for the world famous La Scala opera house -- pride of the Milanese -- while much needed restoration work is carried out.
But Formentini is credited with restoring honesty and transparency to the city hall after a succession of graft-ridden administrations in the 1980s.
"I have to give him his due for one thing and that is honesty," said Massimo Moratti, one of Milan's foremost industrialists who also owns the Internazionale football club.
"But he has never had a great design, he lacks a broad vision," Moratti told Rome daily La Repubblica.

Polls show the Freedom Alliance's Gabriele Albertini having the edge over the Olive Tree's Aldo Fumagalli. Both men are businessmen who promise to create an investment-friendly environment by cleaning up the city.

Albertini, who has run a lacklustre campaign, has said he wants to draft 600 more policemen into the city to help fight rising crime. Fumagalli promises to cut unemployment -- below the national average at 8.2 percent -- by investing heavily in a congress centre and a civic library.
Formentini has played on anti-immigrant feelings by loudly refusing to give temporary accommodation for Albanian refugees.
